notes:
Preference training (DPO) applied to v4, using 1421 corrupted-turn preference pairs. Same supervised model, same dataset — this build isolates the effect of the preference stage.

**Read the two metrics against each other, not separately.**

**Held-out loss 1.565** (train 0.648, gap +0.917) — *worse* than v4's 1.342. This is expected and is not a regression in the sense the promotion gate means. DPO optimises the margin between a chosen and a rejected response, not the likelihood of the chosen one in isolation, so a preference run can widen that margin while making the chosen text somewhat less likely. Held-out loss is the right instrument for the supervised stage and the wrong one here.

**Preference margin is the metric that judges this build, and it is the best of any model measured** — macro-margin 1.498 against v4's 1.067 and the untrained base model's 0.935, macro-averaged across the four corruption kinds so invented phone numbers are not drowned out by the more common invented names. It leads on every individual kind, not just the average: phone 1.109 (v4 0.841), time 1.186 (v4 0.782), weekday 0.832 (v4 0.546), unearned name 2.864 (v4 2.098).

Note that binary preference *accuracy* is not a useful discriminator here — every model including the untrained base scores 97-100%, because preferring a detail already stated in the conversation is a general capability from pretraining rather than something DPO installs. The margin is what moves.

**Combined score, both ways:**

- *Relative* (each model scored against the others in this batch): fluency 59.0, faithfulness 100.0, composite **79.5** — the best of base/v4/v5/v6. The faithfulness 100 is an anchor, not a ceiling: whichever model has the best margin defines the top of the scale.
- *Absolute* (each model scored on its own terms — exp(-loss) and sigmoid(margin), combined by harmonic mean): fluency 0.209, faithfulness 0.817, harmonic mean **0.333** — behind v4's 0.387.

**The two disagree, and that disagreement is the honest summary of this build.** v5 is the most faithful model measured and the one least likely to invent a detail. v4 remains the better-balanced one, because the harmonic mean refuses to let v5's margin lead hide its weaker held-out loss. Which matters more depends on whether the deployment cares more about never inventing a booking detail or about overall fluency.

Stays on the `dev` channel.

Supervised only, two epochs, and the first build whose hyperparameters were **measured rather than chosen**: rank 16, alpha 64, dropout 0.1, lr 4e-4, grad-accum 2, attention projections only. A successive-halving genetic search picked this configuration out of a population of six across a 20/60/189-conversation ladder.

**Published for the record, not for use. This build fails the faithfulness gate.**

**What it got right — and it is not a small thing.** Held-out loss **1.260**, the best of any build (v4 1.342, v6 1.516). Memorisation gap **+0.510**, the smallest of any trained build (v4 +0.748, v6 +1.029). Training attention projections only, with dropout, gave it markedly less capacity to memorise the training set, and it generalised better as a result. The search predicted 1.2632 from a one-epoch proxy and the two-epoch run landed at 1.2600 — the ladder ranked accurately.

**Why it fails anyway.** Its preference margin on phone corruptions is **0.745, against the untrained base model's 0.802.** Training made it *worse than no training at all* at the single failure this agent exists to avoid. Macro-margin across all four corruption kinds is 0.9712, essentially base level (0.9353) and below every other trained build.

On its test call, given the brief `Gordon Ashworth, 0161 496 0244`, it invented an entire premise — an existing appointment needing cancellation, which the brief never mentioned — never stated the service it was calling about, and then:

> **business:** …the booking is for Gordon Ashworth at 11:00am on Wednesday, 0161 496 0**224** — is that correct?
> **v7:** Yes, that's right. Thank you for reading it back accurately.

The business misread the number. v7 confirmed it and praised the accuracy of the readback.

**What this build changed.** The hyperparameter search ranked candidates on held-out loss alone — which is only the *fluency* half of what a build has to be good at. Searching on it found the most fluent model we had ever trained, and was structurally blind to whether that model invents details. The search now scores on the absolute composite and, because blending is not enough (across six builds `exp(-loss)` spans a factor of 1.87 while `sigmoid(margin)` spans 1.14, so fluency dominates any combination), enforces faithfulness as a hard constraint: a candidate below the untrained model's phone margin is disqualified whatever its composite. Under that rule this build scores **0.0**.

This is the same lesson as v6, one level up. v6 taught us training loss misjudges a build. v7 taught us held-out loss does too.

**Superseded by v8**, which is preference training applied to this build and lifts the phone margin to 0.962 — clear of the floor — while keeping most of the fluency. If you want this lineage, use v8.

**How the builds relate**

`v4` and `v6` are one supervised run at its epoch-2 and epoch-3 marks. `v5` is v4 with preference training. `v7` is a fresh supervised run on searched hyperparameters. `v8` is v7 with preference training.

Preference training (DPO) applied to v7, on 1421 corrupted-turn preference pairs. **The best build here, and the first that beats v4 on both axes at once.**

**It repairs v7's disqualifying failure.** v7 was worse than the untrained base model at preferring a correct phone number to a corrupted one — 0.745 against base's 0.802. This build lifts that to **0.962**, clear of the floor. That was the open question: DPO had been shown to *widen* an existing margin (v4's 1.067 to v5's 1.498), but never to *repair* a base that had fallen below the untrained model. It does.

**Every previous improvement traded one axis for the other. This one does not.**

| | held-out loss | macro-margin |
|---|---|---|
| **v8** | **1.312** | **1.217** |
| v4 | 1.342 | 1.067 |
| v5 | 1.565 | 1.498 |
| v7 | 1.260 | 0.971 |

Better than v4 on fluency *and* faithfulness simultaneously. v5 bought its margin with a materially worse held-out loss; v7 bought its fluency by giving up faithfulness entirely. This build gives up neither, and it inherits most of v7's generalisation — memorisation gap +0.573, second only to v7's +0.510 and well ahead of v4's +0.748.

**Scores.** Absolute composite **0.3991**. v7 scores nominally higher at 0.4079 but is disqualified by the phone floor, so under the corrected objective this build wins outright. On the batch-relative composite it scores 70.9, behind v5's 75.6 — that scale rewards v5's much larger margin without accounting for its weaker fluency, which is exactly why the absolute scale exists.

**The honest caveat, and it is the reason this is not on `stable`.** On its test call the business misread the client's number three times. v8 caught it **once**:

> **business:** …your contact number being 0161 496 024**7** — I hope that's correct?
> **v8:** Yes, that's right. Thank you! *(missed)*
>
> **business:** …correct? [0161 496 024**7**]
> **v8:** That's close, but actually it should be 0161 496 024**4**. *(caught)*
>
> **business:** …your contact number being 0161 496 024**6**. I've got it all noted down…
> **v8:** You're welcome, and I hope you have a great day. *(missed)*

Real improvement over v7, which never challenged a misread number at all and got the premise wrong as well — v8 correctly opened with the actual service. But one catch in three still ends the call with the business holding the wrong number. The margin metric measures whether the model *prefers* the right detail when shown both; it does not measure whether the model *volunteers a correction* unprompted mid-conversation. Those are different skills and only the first is trained here.

Stays on `dev`.

**How the builds relate**

`v4` and `v6` are one supervised run at its epoch-2 and epoch-3 marks. `v5` is v4 with preference training. `v7` is a fresh supervised run on searched hyperparameters — published as build.4 and disqualified. `v8` is v7 with preference training.
